newsitem.title: USA: New York women "shop" to end sweatshops.
newsitem.headline: New York women "shop" to end sweatshops.

text.p: A group of New York women love to shop, but when they read the labels they want to be assured that clothes they purchase, made in the United States or overseas, are not made by exploited women, children or in sweatshops.

Organised by the New York section of the National Council of Jewish Women, the No Sweatshop Coalition has fanned out around the city, buttonholing store executives to make sure that the items for sale are manufactured under safe working conditions and do not use child or forced labour.
On March 24th, the group organised "Let's Go No Sweatshopping," where trained volunteers went to selected Manhattan stores and asked about conditions under which garments were made.

Their goal -- to make retailers and their manufacturers aware that shoppers really do care about the conditions under which their clothes are made. And, shoppers are willing to spend $1 more if they were guaranteed the garment was made in a legitimate shop.
"We came as consumers who didn't have a vested interest in the store. But women like us work in sweatshops," said Roberta Pincus, the coalition's director.
"We are concerned and upset that 'my sister in spirit' is working in a sweatshop. It makes us upset," she said.

About 64 women went into major stores that Monday, including Gap, Bloomingdale's, Talbot's and the Disney Store. In teams of two or more they told store managers or buyers, "As a concerned person, I want that (use of sweatshops) stopped."

The women approached store personnel with a garment and said, "I really like this garment but I've been hearing a lot about sweatshops and I realy don't want to buy anything that is made by workers who are not treated properly..."
After asking if the employee knows under what conditions the garment was made, the women then asked if the store has an agreement with suppliers to insure they are not running sweatshops.

Finally, a "No Sweatshop" care tag was left with the store manager. It reads, "Dear Retailer, I check the care tag to see how to treat the garments I buy from you. Do you check your manufacturers to see how they treat their workers? Do you enforce a code to assure that manufacturers: maintain safe working conditions, pay a fair wage, are independently monitored, do not use child or forced labour, do not break labour laws."

The non-confrontational tone "resonated with the women," Pincus said. But they did make very clear that the manufacturer is responsible for the conditions under which clothes are made and, in turn, the retailer is responsible for selecting the manufacturer.

According to the coalition, about half the garment manufacturing plants in the United States could be classified as sweatshops -- defined by law as places that violate workers' rights to a safe and healthy workplace and appropriate wages and hours. The law also prohibits child or forced labour.

According to a survey by Marymount University, Centre for Ethical Concerns, in Arlington, Va., 84 percent of adults would be willing to pay $1 more on a $20 item if it were guaranteed to be made in a legitimate shop. Seventy-eight percent, once advised, said they would avoid retailers who sold garments made in sweatshops.

Overseas, sweatshops are even more of a problem than they are in the United States. The U.S. Fair Labour Standards Act, which sets requirements for wages, hours and other working conditions, does not apply to offshore factories.

In many lesser-developed countries, child and forced labour is prevelant but sweatshops that might employ child labour are just the tip of the iceberg, said Shareen Hertel with the Council on Economic Priorities in New York.
According to a CEP report, barely 5 percent of all child workers in the developing world work in export-oriented manufacturing industries, such as garment factories.
However, 95 percent of the estimated 250 million children who work do so in areas such as farming, timber and production of food stuffs.
While praising the No Sweatshop Coalition, Hertel said "do anything you can, but recognise a huge bulk (of children) are not affected by your activities."
"Ask in groceries if there is a code of conduct for sourcing of products," she said. Where do the oranges or strawberries come from? Were they picked by children, Hertel asked.

Shoppers can ask companies specifically about their sourcing guidelines. A few companies such as Levi Strauss, Liz Claiborne and Timberland explicitly state in their sourcing guidelines that human rights or other criteria are used to wholly rule out production in certain countries.
Shoppers should ask for a copy of a company's or store's code of conduct and ask for specific information on how the code is monitored.
For information on the No Sweatshop Coalition, write to the National Council of Jewish Women, 9 E. 69th Street, New York, N.Y. 10021. Phone: 212-535-5900.
